title: Diamondbacks’ Torey Lovullo apologizes to Cubs after sign-relaying spat: ‘I stand corrected’
content:
PHOENIX — In the end, the Chicago Cubs did nothing wrong.

Defusing a sign-stealing controversy, Arizona Diamondbacks manager Torey Lovullo reached out to his Chicago counterpart, Craig Counsell, after a screaming match between coaches on both sides Monday night popped up on the TV broadcast and then went viral on social media.

Diamondbacks starter Merrill Kelly had escalated the situation after their 7-0 loss at Chase Field, calling it “a little bulls—” and “a little bush league” that Cubs third-base coach Quintin Berry appeared to be relaying information to hitters from his post.

Upon further review, Lovullo indicated he received a satisfactory explanation from Michael Hill, Major League Baseball’s senior vice president of on-field operations, which apparently absolved the Cubs.

“I stand corrected,” Lovullo told reporters ahead of Tuesday’s game. “I had a chance to call ‘Couns’ and apologize to him. I told him that we were wrong and they were doing everything right.

“It’s a very intense time of the year, and a lot goes on. It’s two teams trying to protect their turf. (Counsell) got it, hung up the phone and (we) went our ways and told them that I’d take care of our clubhouse, which I did.”

Tempers flared during the fifth inning Monday, when Kelly said he felt like whenever he threw a changeup, Berry was tipping off Chicago’s hitters, particularly its left-handed batters.

From the dugout, Diamondbacks bench coach Jeff Banister wagged his finger at the Cubs. Chicago bench coach Ryan Flaherty yelled right back across the field. Diamondbacks pitching coach Brian Kaplan also grew animated and seemed to gesture toward Berry in the coach’s box.

“Everything the Chicago Cubs were doing was perfectly legal and within the boundaries of the rules,” Lovullo said. “Yes, they were (relaying information), and good for them. They did a good coaching job; they took advantage of one of our vulnerabilities. Merrill was giving away a couple of his pitches, and the base coaches were relaying it to the hitter or the base runner.”

In the wake of the Houston Astros’ sign-stealing scandal and technology’s takeover of the sport, clubs have been on edge when it comes to opponents relaying information on pitcher tendencies, grips and tells.

“Everybody’s paranoid,” Berry said. “It happens to us all the time. You’re always like, ‘Is there something? Can we clean up on our side? Do they have something?’ That’s the way the game is. Everybody’s thinking about it. Everybody’s trying to keep their house clean. You worry about that. You can’t control anything else.”

Though the Astros were using a sophisticated system that included trash cans, the Cubs studied widely accessible video to find an existing tell on Kelly and relay that in real time.

As Lovullo said, “You can study and prepare for it and give information to people that are on the field, which includes base coaches, so it’s within the rules.”

“It’s just gamesmanship going on back and forth,” Flaherty said. “At the end of the day, we’re responsible for what our team is doing, not what the other team is doing.”

The advent of PitchCom has, for the most part, shifted attention away from a catcher’s fingers and to the person standing 60 feet, 6 inches away. Using multicamera operating systems that can be slowed down in real time, clubs are increasingly finding new ways to gain an edge over the competition, with even the slightest shift by a pitcher potentially providing a lane into understanding what’s coming next.

“We’re constantly looking at our guys so we don’t give away stuff,” Lovullo said. “We slipped, we got beat, and credit to the Cubs for being able to see that.”

In an effort to limit those sight lines, this season MLB tightened a longstanding rule governing where first- and third-base coaches are permitted to stand on the field.

As drawn on the field, the coaching boxes positioned in foul territory look like a three-sided bracket, closed off in every direction except backward, away from the baseline. Those coaches are expected to remain in that area, only moving toward the opposite dugout.

However, with batted balls continuing to travel in excess of 100 mph, base coaches have historically shaded more toward the outfield. Beyond safety, it’s given them a deeper look at the opposing pitcher, potentially confirming existing tells or revealing insights into potential competitive edges.

“This has been going on for a while,” Diamondbacks third baseman Nolan Arenado said. “I’ve played in divisions and different teams where this is happening. You kind of see it, but you don’t know how to expose it. Because it’s not that obvious. I think (Monday) night, some of it was a little bit obvious. It’s something the coaches felt they needed to say.”

Especially when this rule is not always strictly enforced, its intentions can leave things open to interpretation while also causing potential safety concerns for coaches in the line of play.

“That’s what it looked like,” Diamondbacks catcher Gabriel Moreno said. “It looked like they were stealing the signs.”

By letter of the law, Berry was not out of his designated area during Monday’s incident. If he had been, it would have fallen on the umpiring crew to enforce it and the Diamondbacks to flag it.

“It’s just competing, trying to find ways to compete,” Berry said. “When that happens, emotions get high in certain settings. They’re yelling, and I’m yelling back. It’s fine. I have no ill will towards them. I get it.”

The Cubs are led by experienced players, baseball gym rats who enjoy digging into the game’s little details and discussing the finer points of their craft.

“You look for competitive advantages everywhere,” Flaherty said. “A lot of it’s player driven. They care about it. They hold each other accountable. They look for advantages.

“When you’re on the other side of those things, it’s kind of frustrating.”

While the Diamondbacks took batting practice before Tuesday’s game, Banister and Berry laughed together while engaging in a friendly conversation at first base that ended in a hug.

The Diamondbacks moved on with a 5-4 comeback victory. Down 4-0 after seven innings, Arizona scored three runs off Cubs reliever Daniel Palencia, who was upset after hitting Jordan Lawlar’s helmet with a 98.5 mph fastball in the eighth inning. Pinch hitter Ryan Waldschmidt would win it for the Diamondbacks with a two-run, walk-off homer off Cubs closer Jacob Webb.

Baseball is a small world. Lovullo’s son Nick is the bench coach at Chicago’s Triple-A Iowa affiliate, and Counsell’s son Brady was selected by the Diamondbacks in the 10th round of last year’s draft.

“I think the world of Torey,” Counsell said. “He runs a great ship here. I think he’s done a heck of a job, so I enjoy every conversation I get to have with him. So, yeah, he felt like he wanted to do it, and I appreciated it.”
